summary:
Sakarya is a province in Turkey's Marmara region and stands under the national framework: no Sakarya-specific statute, enforcement programme or local ban concerning transgender visitors appears in the sources assembled here, and nationwide provisions govern the province's residents and visitors alike.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, a 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws, leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025 and analysed in Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet. Human Rights Watch's release of 29 October 2025 sets out its terms: conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" would carry up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex ceremonies up to four years. The draft had not been passed when reported in late 2025.

For trans visitors and residents the draft's care provisions carry the sharpest consequences. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add mandatory infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, imprison providers of such care for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have objected to the package.

Amnesty International records the package as the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The organisation warns that it would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights, and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are nationwide proposals and would apply within every province including Sakarya.

Below the draft legislation, the operating environment already reflects state policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions. In Istanbul in 2025 police stopped around 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release, with legal experts arguing that such checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, so any stoppage is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Two further rules bear on a visitor's documents and care. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option on medical-board reports and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
Local authorities have previously used event bans as an instrument against LGBT visibility. Istanbul Pride drew roughly 100,000 participants in 2013 and 2014 before the 2015 to 2018 parades were banned by local authorities, a precedent indicating that a province-level administration in Sakarya could impose comparable restrictions on gatherings even where no such local rule is documented at present.

The pending package sits inside a sequence of failed and revived initiatives. Amnesty International notes two earlier sets of proposed amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025 that stalled in Parliament before the leaked October draft, and notes that enforcement has in places outpaced legislation: the women stopped for GBT checks in Istanbul in 2025 were told of rules that had not yet been enacted. Reporting on the Health Ministry regulation was framed online as an "LGBT opening", a contested characterisation.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need for a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than a statement of current law.

The national baseline is comparatively permissive on its face. Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, which places the current trajectory in contrast with the country's own statutory history rather than with jurisdictions that criminalise same-sex conduct outright.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in Turkey requires a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40. The applicant must be at least 18, unmarried and hold a medical report from a state-designated hospital. The leaked 11th Judicial Package would raise the minimum age for these procedures from 18 to 25 and add further conditions, though it remained a draft when last reported.

Access to transition-related care is governed by medical boards. The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation followed a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, while barring hospitals from recording the "other" option and requiring that reports be issued electronically. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records.

The Turkish military bars homosexuals from service and treats homosexuality as a "psychosexual" illness, a classification that bears on conscription-age residents.

Prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, a case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 that confirmed a trans man had been held in a women's prison. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, reporting that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a Sakarya-specific statute, police instruction, local ban or designated facility concerning transgender visitors. Whether Sakarya police conduct GBT-style identity checks of the kind documented in Istanbul, and how frequently, is unresolved here.

The 11th Judicial Package is a leaked draft, not enacted law. Its terms are as reported by Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International in October and November 2025; whether any provision has since been amended, adopted or withdrawn is not sourced in this inventory, and enforcement ahead of enactment has been reported only from Istanbul.

Whether any hospital in Sakarya holds state-designated status for the medical report required by Civil Code Article 40, and whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation has altered reporting at provincial facilities, is not sourced here.

Cases cited in this record include the death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025. Independent judicial findings on that death were still outstanding at the time of the December 2025 parliamentary question, and no investigation outcome is available in this inventory.

Figures on violations and detentions derive from Kaos GL's national monitoring and are not broken down by province; no Sakarya-specific count of detentions, assaults or hate-crime findings appears in the sources assembled here.
